A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EYES-ON-ME framework and matching core experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison; relocated appendix material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original RAG poisoning experiments, model and trigger transfer evaluations, ablations, and defense evaluations in Sections 5–6 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds AutoDAN results, attention-based defense analyses, and hybrid-variant ablations in Table 1 and Appendices E and G.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same attractor/payload decomposition, correlated-head selection, independently optimized attention objectives, and HotFlip search with fluency filtering. The separate loss equations and expanded pseudocode in v2 document the existing method; they do not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: MS MARCO, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and the existing triggered RAG tasks are retained, including information gathering and URL insertion. The added comparisons and hybrid ablations use retained data and task coverage with additional methods or configurations.

E2.justification: AutoDAN, previously only discussed, is added to the evaluated comparators in Table 1. Appendix E also evaluates Attention Tracker and Normalized Passage Attention Score against the proposed attacks. Existing comparator membership in Table 5 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Existing corpus sizes, top-5 retrieval, model configurations, and optimization budgets are retained. The new defense analysis uses 35 attractor sets, benign passages from the same distribution, and attention-shift and attention-variance metrics. Appendix G applies the existing ablation factors to the hybrid configuration.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends analysis beyond v1's standard-variant ablations and five defenses. Appendix G examines hybrid-variant initialization, instruction complexity, head-selection thresholds, and trigger frequency. Appendix E adds two attention-based detection analyses with benign controls, addressing the attack's detectability.

E5.justification: Both retain the statement that random seeds were fixed where possible, without adding repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 35 attractor sets describe evaluation samples; Table 9's attention variance is a detector metric, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing results in Tables 1–5 are retained, but substantial new outcomes are reported. AutoDAN averages 13.54% with Qwen3-Emb and 14.64% with BCE in Table 1. Tables 9–11 add detector statistics and hybrid ablation results, including 71.78% E2E-ASR for random initialization and 9.71% for URL insertion. These are additional results, not revised scores for retained settings.

T1.justification: The threat-model definitions and attention-mass formulation remain unchanged. v2's Equations 5–6 explicitly restate the independent objectives already described in v1; no new theorem, proof, assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of modularity, reuse, transferability, and 57.8% average attack success across 18 RAG configurations. The new evidence does not redefine the principal contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 expands the explanation of baseline weakness through trigger competition and retrieval rank. Appendix E attributes limited detector response to manipulating a small subset of heads, while Appendix G extends sensitivity interpretations to the hybrid variant. Existing limitations concerning complex instructions, mean pooling, and rerankers remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit source-code link and expands Appendix F with inputs, outputs, head-selection logic, and staged attractor-optimization pseudocode. Most implementation information was already present in v1, including initialization, iteration limits, fluency filtering, hardware, and corpus construction.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hung et al. (2025) and Choudhary et al. (2025) for the attention-based defenses and extends its positioning against those approaches. Discussion of Phantom's trigger assumptions is refined. The broader related-work narrative remains stable; AutoDAN was already cited.

P1.justification: Targeted edits explain HotFlip, expand the algorithm narrative, and revise the baseline discussion. Examples and defense descriptions exchange Appendix D/E positions, and the header changes to 'Preprint.' Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 8 gain AutoDAN entries, and Tables 9–11 display the new analyses. The compact algorithm display labeled Figure 6 in v1 becomes expanded Algorithms 1–3. Existing scientific figures remain unchanged, with localized caption, placement, and pagination adjustments.

improvement.justification: Adding AutoDAN to the main comparison and testing the hybrid variant's sensitivities strengthens validation of the configuration underlying the headline result. The code-access link and expanded pseudocode also improve inspectability. The overall gain is limited: core findings remain unchanged, and the new defense-evasion interpretation rests on aggregate attention scores without detection rates or uncertainty estimates.
